To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the phoretic velocity of a particle is the sum of a back-flow contribution and an indirect Brownian and solute pressure contribution.

the phoretic motion of a particle driven by an imposed solute concentration gradient is the sum of the back-flow contribution and the indirect contribution, that the back-flow contribution can be neglected in the case of self-phoresis (i.e. autonomous motion), and that the velocity of a particle undergoing self-propulsion can be written in a simple form in terms of a surface integral of the ‘solute pressure’.

(i) diffusiophoretic motion is a consequence of the chemical potential gradient acting on the solute particles, which in turn induces a hydrodynamic disturbance in the surrounding fluid, (ii) the particle velocity results from the balance of the chemical potential and interparticle forces on the particle with the Stokes drag of solvent, (iii) the velocity of self-phoretic motion is the integral of the ‘solute pressure’, the solute concentration multiplied by the thermal energy, over the surface

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
phoresis is a consequence of the balance of the hydrodynamic stress and chemical potential gradient force with the solutes and the balance of the Brownian and intermolecular forces with the solute.

diffusiophoresis is a consequence of the combined action of two forces: the chemical potential gradient acting on the solute (or solute gradient force acting on the phoresis particle) and the mutual interparticle force acting on the solutes and the phoretic particles.

the phoretic motion of a particle driven by an external concentration gradient of a small solute species is a consequence of the long-range hydrodynamics of the solute, which is a consequence of Brownian motion and interparticle forces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the colloidal perspective provides a more general description of diffusiophoretic motion, but the two approaches are complementary and the continuum approach can be used to provide the hydrodynamic velocity disturbance that is the starting point of the colloidal approach.

diffusiophoresis can be understood as a form of Brownian motion in which the Brownian forces are replaced by chemical potential gradient forces and the Brownian particles are replaced by solute particles, with the result that the Brownian motion is replaced by a phoretic motion.
the continuum approach is valid for a particle much larger than the solute and at very low solute concentrations, while the colloidal approach is valid for any size ratio and concentration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the phoretic velocity is a balance of the forces on the phoretizer (the phoretic particle), and the velocity of the phoretizer is the result of that force balance.

the continuum approach is only valid for a dilute solute and a large particle, whereas the colloidal approach can treat any size ratio and concentration of solute and provides an alternative mechanical analysis of phoretic and self-propulsive motion.
the phoretic motion of a particle is a complex interplay of the hydrodynamic and chemical interactions of the solute with the particle.
